s: A. Enumerated powers and necessary-and-proper means.
The first question about any federal statute is "Where does Congress get the power?"
Congress has no general police power.

United States v. Lopez (1995) and NFIB v. Sebelius (2012) both stressed that reading any power so broadly as to supply one would collapse the distinction "between what is truly national and what is truly local."
The Necessary and Proper Clause (Art. I, § 8, cl. 18) lets Congress choose the means for executing its enumerated powers.
In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), Chief Justice Marshall read "necessary" to mean "convenient" or "useful," not "absolutely necessary."
Congress could therefore charter a national bank as a means to its taxing, borrowing and war powers.
United States v. Comstock (2010) upheld civil commitment of sexually dangerous federal prisoners as a "rational" means "reasonably adapted" to legitimate ends.
NFIB added that a law must also be "proper," meaning consistent with the Constitution's structure.
A law that creates a new, independent power (such as compelling commerce) is not merely incidental.
Valid federal law displaces conflicting state law (see Preemption, Part V).
McCulloch also held that states may not tax federal instrumentalities, because "the power to tax involves the power to destroy."
Is a federal statute within Congress's power?
Identify the enumerated power relied on (commerce, tax, spending, § 5, war, and so on).
Is the statute itself an exercise of that power?
If not, is it a necessary and proper means: rationally related and reasonably adapted to executing that power?
Is it "proper": does it respect federalism and other structural limits (anti-commandeering, sovereign immunity)?
Does it violate any independent constitutional limit, such as an individual right?
